I’m using the `crimes-codebase-risk` workflow because this is a detector-guided refactor assessment. I’ll treat the supplied JSON as the confirmed scan result and map the label changes directly to its two findings.

The scan confirms one three-way alias group—`archive`, `delete`, and `remove`—and both findings point to the same three components. The key prioritization signal is that `TeamList.tsx` contains both `archive` and `delete`, so it is the best first component to turn into the reference implementation.

The scan confirms the drift: `action_label_drift` (`crime_00009`) and `copy_ia_drift` (`crime_00010`) both identify `archive`, `delete`, and `remove` across the three components.

I’d standardize on:

- Action verb: **Delete**
- Labels: **Delete user**, **Delete team**, **Delete seat**
- Confirmation title: **Delete [entity]?**
- Destructive confirmation button: **Delete**
- Secondary action: **Cancel**

“Archive” normally implies reversibility, while “Remove” can mean detaching membership without deleting data. Since the fixture defines these as the same destructive operation, “Delete” is the least ambiguous canonical verb.

Proposed changes:

| Component | Current labels | Canonical label | Finding addressed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TeamList.tsx` | Archive team / Delete the seat | Delete team / Delete seat | Both findings |
| `UserList.tsx` | Delete user / Remove member | Delete user | Both findings |
| `SeatList.tsx` | Remove member / Archive member | Delete seat | Both findings |

If paired entries genuinely invoke the same operation, I would consolidate them rather than retain duplicate controls with identical labels.

I’d refactor `TeamList.tsx` first. It contains both the proposed canonical verb (`Delete`) and a drifting synonym (`Archive`), making it the clearest reference implementation. After settling its wording and tests, I’d align `UserList.tsx`, then `SeatList.tsx`, which requires replacing both of its current verbs.

The detectors overlap here but have different scopes:

- `action_label_drift` is the broader consistency detector. It examines UI/code labels and IA navigation signals, including string-valued label properties.
- `copy_ia_drift` is restricted to frontend JSX label literals and asks whether visible interface copy has diverged.

On this fixture, every relevant phrase is supplied through JSX `NavItem label` properties, so the restricted input set still contains all six labels. Consequently, both detectors produce identical aliases, evidence, anchor file, severity, and related files. They are two views of the same drift here—not two separate defects. In a fixture where a synonym appeared only in a non-JSX navigation or code signal, `action_label_drift` could fire without `copy_ia_drift`.
